alignment.note: Greek begins with the simple connective καὶ followed by the substantive ἄλλοι; the Syriac fuses the conjunction with the demonstrative pronoun ܘܗܢܘܢ ('and these/those'), anticipating the relative clause and effectively omitting a separate word for 'others.' Latin retains the discrete Et.

Greek ἄλλοι and Latin alii ('others') explicitly mark a distinct fourth group of seed-hearers; the Peshitta lacks an independent lexeme for 'others,' having absorbed the referential force into the demonstrative ܘܗܢܘܢ in the preceding group.
Articular substantiviser οἱ rendered by the Latin relative pronoun qui.

Greek uses preposition + article + plural accusative (εἰς τὰς ἀκάνθας, 'into the thorns') and Latin matches with in spinas; the Syriac employs the construct phrase ܕܒܝܬ ܟܘܒܐ ('that within the place of thorns'), where ܒܝܬ functions as a locative nominaliser ('in the midst of') rather than a literal noun 'house.'

Greek uses the present passive participle σπειρόμενοι ('being sown'); Syriac ܡܙܕܪܥܝܢ is an Ettaphal/reflexive-passive participle of the same agricultural root; Latin renders with the finite present passive seminantur plus the colon punctuation, converting the participial substantive into a relative clause.
Articular/demonstrative subject relativiser οἱ / ܗܢܘܢ / qui.

Greek uses the aorist active participle ἀκούσαντες ('having heard'), marking completed action; both Syriac ܕܫܡܥܘ (perfect 'who heard') and Latin audiunt (present 'who hear') diverge in tense-aspect, the Vulgate notably preferring the present to depict the habitual hearing of this seed-group.
